titleStmt.title: An improved global EDF schedulability test for uniform multiprocessors *

analytic.title: An improved global EDF schedulability test for uniform multiprocessors *

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The global EDF scheduling of sporadic task systems upon uniform multiprocessor platforms is studied. A new sufficient schedulability test is presented and proved correct. Some interesting issues are discussed, that arise regarding the choice of an appropriate metric for evaluating the test quantitatively. Metrics based on processor speedup factor are proposed, and the test is quantitatively evaluated in terms of these metrics.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: A uniform multiprocessor platform is comprised of multiple processors, which may differ from each other only in the rate at which they can execute work. More specifically, each processor is characterized by a speed or computing capacity ρ parameter and any job executing on the processor for t time units completes t × ρ units of execution.

In the sporadic task model, a real-time task system is modeled as a finite collection of sporadic tasks. Each sporadic task τ i is characterized by three parameters: τ i = (C i , D i , T i ), with the interpretation that τ i may generate an infinite sequence of jobs with successive jobs arriving at least T i time units apart, each with an execution requirement at most C i and a deadline D i time-units after its arrival time. Sporadic task systems in which each task is required to have its relative deadline and period parameters the same (D i = T i for all i) are called implicit-deadline task systems, and ones in which each task is required to have its relative deadline be no larger than its period parameter (D i ≤ T i for all i) are called constrained-deadline task systems.

In this paper, we study the scheduling of sporadic task systems upon uniform multiprocessor platforms. We as-sume that the platform is fully preemptive, -an executing job may be interrupted at any instant in time and have its execution resumed later with no cost or penalty. We study the behavior of the well-known Earliest Deadline First scheduling algorithm when scheduling systems of sporadic tasks upon such preemptive platforms. We assume that the platform allows for global inter-processor migration -a job may begin execution on any processor and a preempted job may resume execution on the same processor as, or a different processor from, the one it had been executing on prior to preemption. (However, each job may execute on at most one processor at each instant in time.) We will refer to Earliest Deadline First scheduling with global interprocessor migration as global EDF (or simply EDF).

Related work. To our knowledge, only one other paper - [5] -has studied the global EDF scheduling of sporadic task systems on uniform multiprocessor platforms. A test was derived there for determining whether a given constraineddeadline sporadic task system is guaranteed to be scheduled to meet all deadlines upon a specified uniform multiprocessor platform, when scheduled using global EDF. This test was evaluated qualitatively, and was shown to be a generalization of prior tests for EDF schedulability analysis on uniprocessors and identical multiprocessors (these are a special case of uniform multiprocessors, in which all processors have the same speed).

Contributions. One of the drawbacks of the test in [5] was the lack of quantitative analysis. In this paper, we address this drawback by designing a schedulability test (different from the one in [5]), for which we are able to derive quantitative performance guarantees in the form of processor speedup factors.

In addition to the schedulability test itself, we believe that some interesting choices are available regarding this choice of a metric for quantitative evaluation. The processor speedup factor metric typically evaluates the effectiveness of a schedulability test by comparing its effectiveness on a platform as compared to the effectiveness of a hypothetical optimal test on a slower platform. For uniform multiprocessor platforms, in which each processor may have a different speed, it is not quite clear how this comparison should be done. We have essentially considered two reasonable alternatives here -one in which the optimal test has a slower identical multiprocessor platform, and one in which the optimal test has a uniform multiprocessor platform in which the speed of all the processors is scaled down by the same factor.

Organization. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we formally define the sporadic task model and uniform multiprocessors platforms, and provide some additional useful definitions, notation, and terminology concerning sporadic tasks and uniform multiprocessors. We also briefly discuss how global EDF is to be implemented upon uniform multiprocessors. In Section 3 we derive, and prove the correctness of, a schedulability test for determining whether a given constrained-deadline sporadic task system is EDF-schedulable on a specified uniform multiprocessor platform. In Section 4, we evaluate the efficacy of our schedulability test qualitatively, using the metric of processor speedup factor.. To our knowledge, this metric has not been previously applied to the analysis of scheduling algorithms on uniform multiprocessor platforms, hence we have to define the scope of the technique here prior to being able to apply it. More specifically, we end up defining the processor speedup factor in two plausible ways, and evaluate our sufficient schedulability test according to both these metrics.

2 Task and platform model §1. Sporadic task systems. As briefly mentioned in Section 1, a sporadic task τ i = (C i , D i , T i ) is characterized by a worst-case execution requirement C i , a (relative) deadline D i , and a minimum inter-arrival separation parameter T i , also referred to as the period of the task. Such a sporadic task generates a potentially infinite sequence of jobs, with successive job-arrivals separated by at least T i time units. Each job has a worst-case execution requirement equal to C i and a deadline that occurs D i time units after its arrival time. We refer to the interval, of size D i , between such a job's arrival instant and deadline as its scheduling window. We assume a fully preemptive execution model: any executing job may be interrupted at any instant in time, and its execution resumed later with no cost or penalty. A sporadic task system is comprised of a finite number of such sporadic tasks. Let τ denote a system of such sporadic tasks: τ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . τ n }, with τ i = (C i , D i , T i ) for all i, 1 ≤ i ≤ n. Task system τ is said to be a constrained sporadic task system if it is guaranteed that each task τ i ∈ τ has its relative deadline parameter no larger than its period: D i ≤ T i for all τ i ∈ τ . We restrict our attention here to constrained task systems.

div.p: Earliest Deadline First scheduling. Priority-driven scheduling algorithms operate on uniform multiprocessors as follows: at each instant in time they assign a priority to each job that is awaiting execution, and favor for execution the jobs with the greatest priorities. Specifically, (i) no processor is idled while there is an active job awaiting execution; (ii) when there are fewer active jobs than processors, the jobs execute on the fastest processors and the slowest ones are idled; and (iii) greater-priority jobs execute on the faster processors. The Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling algorithm [14,11] is a priority-driven scheduling algorithm that assigns priority to jobs according to their (absolute) deadlines: the earlier the deadline, the greater the priority.

With respect to a given platform, a given sporadic task system is said to be feasible if there exists a schedule meeting all deadlines for every collection of jobs that may be generated by the task system. A given sporadic task system is said to be (global) EDF schedulable if EDF meets all deadlines for every collection of jobs that may be generated by the task system.

div.head: A quantitative evaluation
div.p: Processor speedup factors represent a quantitative approach towards comparing different sufficient schedulability tests. A schedulability test is defined to have a processor speedup factor f , f ≥ 1, if any task system not deemed to be schedulable by this test upon a particular platform is guaranteed to not be feasible -schedulable by an optimal clairvoyant scheduler -upon a platform that is at most 1/f times as fast.

Informally speaking, the processor speedup factor of a schedulability test quantifies both the pessimism of the test and the non-optimality of the scheduling algorithm. According to this metric, schedulability tests with smaller processor speedup factors are superior to ones with larger processor speedup factors, with a processor speedup factor equal to one implying both that the scheduling algorithm is optimal and that the test is exact.

It is reasonable to ask whether it makes sense to bundle both the non-optimality of the scheduling algorithm and the pessimism of the test into a single metric. From a pragmatic perspective, we believe that the answer is "yes" for our domain of interest, which is hard-real-time systems. Since it must be a priori guaranteed in such hard-real-time systems that all deadlines will be met during run-time, a scheduling algorithm is only as good as its associated schedulability test. In other words, a scheduling algorithm, no matter how close to optimal, cannot be used in the absence of an associated schedulability test able to guarantee that all deadlines will be met; what matters is that the combination of scheduling algorithm and schedulability test together have desirable properties.

To the best of our knowledge, prior work in real-time scheduling on processor speedup factors have only considered uniprocessor [4,10] or identical multiprocessor [9,3] platforms. In this section, our goal is to extend the concept of processor speedup factors to be applicable to uniform multiprocessor platforms as well. There appears to be two fairly intuitive way of going about with this: comparing the behavior of the scheduling algorithm on the given platform with that of an optimal algorithm upon a slower identical multiprocessor platform, or on a slower uniform multiprocessor platform in which each processor is slower by the same factor. We explore the first approach in Section 4.1, and the second one in Section 4.2.

Most research on multiprocessor real-time scheduling has focused on the simplest model -systems of implicitdeadline tasks that are scheduled on identical multiprocessors. More recent research has attempted to generalize this work in two different directions, by either generalizing the task model (to constrained-deadline and arbitrary-deadline sporadic task systems), or by generalizing the processor model (to uniform and unrelated multiprocessors). To our knowledge, [5] was the first work that generalized along both the task-model and the processor axes, by considering the scheduling of constrained-deadline sporadic task systems upon uniform multiprocessors. A sufficient schedulability condition for global EDF of constrained-deadline sporadic task systems upon uniform multiprocessors was derived and evaluated qualitatively in [5]. In this paper, we have continued along this line of research by seeking schedulability conditions that can be evaluated in a quantitative manner. We have derived a new schedulability test, that uses the FF-LOAD and δ max parameters of a task system and the total capacity and the λ parameter of a platform to determine the schedulability of the task system upon the platform. This test differs substantially from the one in [5], in that it is based on algorithmic techniques unknown at the time work described in [5] was performed. We have obtained a quantitative evaluation of the effectiveness of our new schedulability test, in terms of the processor speedup factor metric; this, too, continues a recent trend from research into schedulability analysis upon identical multiprocessors.

In some recent research [8,7], Bini et al. have explored ideas that are related to scheduling on uniform multiprocessors. They consider platforms comprised of several identical processors, but under the assumption that not all processors are always available; hence, over an appropriately large time-interval, the total amount of computing capacity available on each processor is different. We recognize that analysis on such a model is considerably more difficult than analysis on the dedicated uniform multiprocessor platforms considered here; it would nevertheless be interesting to explore whether the techniques introduced here extend to such a model as well.

div.head: Appendix: The lambda parameter
div.p: Recall that a uniform multiprocessor π is assumed to be comprised of m(π) > 1 processors with the i'th-fastest processor having speed ρ i (π), and that R(π) denotes the sum of the computing capacities of all the processors in π.
We had claimed that an additional parameter, called the lambda parameter:
div.formula: λ(π) def = m(π) max i=1 m(π) j=i+1 ρ j (π) ρ i (π) .
div.p: is useful for characterizing π. Below, we attempt to provide a justification for this claim. Many derivations of schedulability conditions for global scheduling algorithms proceed as follows:
1. Consider a schedule in which some deadline is missed at some time-instant t d .

2. Identify some interval [t a , t d ) over which the total execution requirement by all the tasks in the system being scheduled must exceed the total execution occurring over this interval, in order for such a deadline miss to occur. Different schedulability tests differ in the value they assign to t a ; for example, the test in [6] (for identical multiprocessors) sets t a to be the arrival time of the job that missed its deadline, while the test in [2] (also for identical multiprocessors) sets t a to be the earliest time-instant prior to t d at which a certain load condition is satisfied. This interval is defined in such a manner that at each instant in the interval, there is guaranteed to be some job or the other that is activehas arrived but not completed execution.
3. Determine an upper bound U on the total execution requirement over [t a , t d ), and a lower bound L on the total execution occurring over [t a , t d ).
4. For a deadline miss to occur, it is necessary that L > U; hence, L ≤ U is a sufficient schedulability condition.

We illustrate for the simple test of [6], in which t a is set equal to the arrival time of the job (say, of task τ k ) that missed its deadline at t d . (Since this job misses its deadline, it is clearly active at each instant within [t a , t d ).)

Determining the lower bound L on the amount of execution occurring over [t a , t d ) is equivalent to determining an upper bound on the amount for which processors are idled over [t a , t d ). No processor can be idled while τ k 's job is not executing, since τ k 's job, being active throughout the interval, would execute whenever a processor is available. Hence some processors may be idled only while τ k 's job is executing; since this job does not complete, it executes for strictly less than C k .

• For the identical multiprocessor case, let us assume that the speed of each processor is equal to one. C k is thus a strict upper bound on the length of time for which one or more processors idles. Assuming that all the (m -1) other processors idle during this time, the lower bound L is given by (mD k -(m -1)C k ).

• For the uniform multiprocessor case, let us denote by ∆ i the sum of the intervals for which (m(π) -i) processors are idled over [t a , t d ), for each i ≥ 1. By the definition of global EDF on uniform multiprocessors, it is always the case that the slowest processors are idled. Hence the fastest i processors -those with speeds ρ 1 (π), ρ 2 (π), . . . , ρ i (π) -are executing during these intervals. As observed above, τ k 's job must be executing on some processor during these intervals; hence, it completes at least ∆ i × ρ i (π) units of execution, while the amount of idled processor capacity is equal to ∆ i × m(π) j=i+1 ρ j (π). In other words, idling (m(π) -i) processors idles capacity proportional to m(π) j=i+1 ρ j (π), while "consuming" an amount of τ k 's job proportional to ρ i (π). To maximize the amount of idled capacity subject to the constraint that τ k 's job execute for strictly less than C k units, therefore, we should idle (m(π) -i) processors for that value of i that maximizes the ratio m(π) j=i+1 ρ j (π) ρ i (π) .

Observe that this is exactly the definition of λ(π), as given by Equation 2. The justification for this definition is now immediate: this is an upper bound on the rate at which capacity can be idled while "consuming" the capacity of some executing job.

If we are to choose to idle this many processors, the lower bound L on the amount of work done over the interval [t a , t d ) becomes equal to (R(π)D k -λ(π)C k ) , which helps explain why the lambda parameter λ(π) seems a critical distinguishing characteristic of the platform π, at least from the perspective of worst-case analysis.
